items.prompt: What causes a rainbow to form in the sky?

options.label: Reflection of light off a flat surface
options.feedback: A rainbow needs water droplets, not a flat surface. It forms when light enters, bounces inside, and leaves a droplet.

options.label: Diffraction of light around a cloud
options.feedback: Diffraction is not what creates a rainbow. The rainbow comes from light bending and reflecting inside spherical water droplets.

options.label: Refraction, internal reflection, and dispersion in water droplets
options.feedback: Correct. Light bends as it enters a droplet, reflects off the inside back, then bends again as it leaves, and dispersion separates the colours.

options.label: Absorption of light by water vapour
options.feedback: Absorption would remove light, not create a bright arc. The rainbow is made by light that passes through droplets and comes back to your eye.

items.ok_line: You know how a rainbow gets its light.
items.ko_line: Think about the path light takes through a raindrop.
items.exp_text: A rainbow is an optical phenomenon caused by light being refracted as it enters a water droplet, reflected inside on the back of the droplet, and refracted again as it leaves. The dispersion separates the white light into its colours, and the result is a continuous spectrum seen as a multicoloured arc.

items.prompt: Where in the sky does a rainbow caused by sunlight always appear?

options.label: Directly in the direction of the Sun
options.feedback: That would put the Sun behind the rainbow, but the bow is actually on the opposite side. If you face a rainbow, the Sun is at your back.

options.label: In the section of sky closest to the horizon on the Sun's side
options.feedback: No, the rainbow is not near the Sun. It appears in the part of the sky directly opposite the Sun, so the Sun must be behind you.

options.label: At the zenith, directly overhead
options.feedback: The rainbow's position depends on where the Sun is, not on a fixed overhead spot. It always shows in the sky opposite the Sun.

options.label: In the section of sky directly opposite the Sun
options.feedback: Correct. Sunlight enters droplets in front of you, and the light returns to your eye from that opposite direction, so the arc appears there.

items.ok_line: You know where to look for a rainbow.
items.ko_line: Remember which side of the sky holds the bow.
items.exp_text: Rainbows caused by sunlight always appear in the section of sky directly opposite the sun. That is why you have to stand with the Sun behind you to see one, and why the centre of the arc lies on a line from the Sun through your eye.

items.prompt: What shape does a rainbow appear to have when viewed from the ground?

options.label: An illuminated arc
options.feedback: Correct. From the ground, the rainbow looks like an arc, because the lower half is hidden below the horizon. Only when flying high can you see the full circle.

options.label: A straight line of colours
options.feedback: No, a rainbow is curved, not straight. It is a circular arc, and its centre lies on the line from the Sun to your eye.

options.label: A complete circle
options.feedback: A full circle is only visible from above the Earth, such as from an aeroplane. From the ground, the bottom part is cut off by the horizon.

options.label: An oval with flattened ends
options.feedback: The rainbow is not an oval. It is a circular arc; the curvature comes from the angle at which light returns from the droplets.

items.ok_line: You see the rainbow's usual shape.
items.ko_line: What cuts off part of the circle from the ground?
items.exp_text: When viewed from the ground, a rainbow typically appears as an illuminated arc. It is actually part of a circle, but the lower half is hidden below the horizon. If you fly high enough in mist, you can see it as a full circle.

options.label: A continuous spectrum of light seen in the sky
options.feedback: Correct. A rainbow is an optical phenomenon showing a continuous spectrum of light in the sky.

options.label: A pattern of colours on the surface of a water droplet
options.feedback: That is not right. The colours appear in the sky, not on the droplet itself.

options.label: A single band of one colour in the air
options.feedback: Wrong. It is a continuous spectrum, meaning many colours appear together, not just one.

options.label: A reflection of the Sun's disc on water
options.feedback: No. That is a reflection, not a rainbow, which involves refraction, internal reflection, and dispersion.

items.ok_line: A rainbow is a spectrum of colours in the sky.
items.ko_line: Think about what appears in the sky.
items.exp_text: A rainbow is an optical phenomenon caused by refraction, internal reflection, and dispersion of light in water droplets. It appears in the sky as a continuous spectrum of colours. It is not a single colour or a reflection; it is a full display of many colours together.

items.prompt: In which part of the sky does a rainbow caused by sunlight appear?

options.label: In the section of sky directly above the Sun
options.feedback: That is not right. A rainbow is never above the Sun; it is on the opposite side of the sky.

options.label: In the section of sky beside the Sun
options.feedback: No. The rainbow is not beside the Sun; it is directly opposite to it.

options.label: In the section of sky directly opposite the Sun
options.feedback: Correct. Sunlit rainbows always appear in the sky opposite to the Sun.

options.label: In the section of sky directly below the Sun
options.feedback: That is wrong. Below the Sun would be the ground, not where a rainbow appears.

items.ok_line: The rainbow is always across from the Sun.
items.ko_line: Think of the Sun and the rainbow facing each other.
items.exp_text: Rainbows caused by sunlight always appear in the section of sky directly opposite the Sun. That is why you look away from the Sun to see one. It is not above, beside, or below the Sun.

items.prompt: When seen from the ground, what shape does a rainbow typically have?

options.label: A full circle
options.feedback: That is wrong. From the ground, a rainbow appears as an arc, not a full circle.

options.label: An illuminated arc
options.feedback: Correct. From the ground, rainbows are seen as an arc, not a complete circle.

options.label: A straight line
options.feedback: No. A rainbow curves; it is not straight.

options.label: A half-circle only in the morning
options.feedback: Wrong. The arc shape is typical regardless of the time of day.

items.ok_line: You see an arc from the ground.
items.exp_text: When viewed from the ground, a rainbow typically appears as an illuminated arc. It is not a full circle from there. In fact, it is only when flying that you might see a full circle, provided there is enough mist.

items.prompt: In a primary rainbow, which colour is on the outer part?

options.label: Red
options.feedback: Correct. In a primary rainbow, red is on the outer part of the arc.

options.label: Violet
options.feedback: That is wrong. Violet is on the inner side, not the outer.

options.label: Blue
options.feedback: No. Blue appears inside the rainbow, not on the outer edge.

options.label: Yellow
options.feedback: That is not right. Yellow is in the middle range, not the outer edge.

items.exp_text: In a primary rainbow, the arc shows red on the outer part and violet on the inner side. This is because light of different wavelengths is bent by different amounts, and red emerges at the larger angle.

items.prompt: What causes the primary rainbow to form?

options.label: Light reflecting off the front surface of the droplet only
options.feedback: Not right. Reflection at the front alone does not make the primary rainbow; there is more happening.

options.label: Light passing straight through the droplet without bending
options.feedback: Wrong. Light is refracted and internally reflected, not just going straight through.

options.label: Light refracted entering a droplet, reflected inside on the back, then refracted again leaving
options.feedback: Correct. This is exactly how the primary rainbow is formed.

options.label: Light bouncing inside the droplet many times before leaving
options.feedback: No. For the primary rainbow, there is only one internal reflection, not multiple bounces.

items.ko_line: Think of the path inside the droplet.
items.exp_text: The primary rainbow is caused by light being refracted when it enters a droplet of water, then reflected inside on the back of the droplet, and refracted again when it leaves. That is the path that produces the primary bow.

items.prompt: In a double rainbow, what is the order of colours in the second arc?

options.label: The same order as the primary rainbow
options.feedback: Wrong. The second arc has its colours reversed compared to the primary.

options.label: It has no colours, just white light
options.feedback: That is not true. The second arc does show colours, but in reverse order.

options.label: Red on the upper side
options.feedback: No. In the second arc, red is on the lower side, not the upper.

options.label: Red on the lower side, with the order reversed
options.feedback: Correct. The second arc shows colours in reverse order, with red on the lower side.

items.ko_line: Look at which side is red.
items.exp_text: In a double rainbow, a second arc appears about 10° outside the primary arc. Its colours are perceived to be in reverse order, with red on the lower side of the arc. So the sequence runs from violet at the top to red at the bottom.

items.prompt: When can a moonbow be seen?

options.label: Only during a solar eclipse
options.feedback: That is wrong. A moonbow has nothing to do with an eclipse.

options.label: On strongly moonlit nights
options.feedback: Correct. Moonbows are rarely seen on strongly moonlit nights.

options.label: Whenever it rains at sunset
options.feedback: No. That would be a sunlit rainbow, not a moonbow.

options.label: Only in winter when the air is very cold
options.feedback: Not right. Cold air is not the condition for a moonbow; strong moonlight is needed.

items.ko_line: Think about what lights up the drops.
items.exp_text: A moonbow, also called a lunar rainbow or nighttime rainbow, can be seen on strongly moonlit nights. Because human colour vision is poor in low light, moonbows are often perceived as white.
